E1-06-natural-selection-flowchart

Flow chart of Darwin's theory of natural selection with seven boxes linked by downward arrows, each with a simple icon. 1: a frog surrounded by many eggs (overproduction). 2: a graph with a flat line (population stays constant). 3: two antelopes competing for a small patch of grass, a lion in the background (struggle for existence). 4: a row of five antelopes with slightly different leg lengths and colours (variation). 5: the faster antelopes escaping a lion while a slower one is caught (survival of the fittest). 6: a fast antelope with its young (inheritance of favourable variations). 7: a branching tree with a new species at the end of a branch (origin of new species).
E1-01-adaptive-radiation-mammal

Adaptive radiation diagram. In the centre, a small shrew-like ancestral mammal. Radiating outwards on curved branching lines are six modern mammals, each in its habitat: a bat flying, a whale swimming, a mole burrowing in soil, a monkey climbing a tree, an antelope running on grassland, and a human walking.
E1-04-lamarck-giraffe-neck-evolution

Lamarck's explanation of the giraffe's neck as three panels in a left-to-right sequence. Panel 1: a short-necked ancestral giraffe stretching its neck upwards towards leaves on a tall acacia tree, with grass bare below. Panel 2: the same giraffe after a lifetime of stretching, with a slightly longer neck, standing beside its young, which is born with an equally longer neck (shown with an arrow from parent to young). Panel 3: after many generations, a modern long-necked giraffe feeding easily on high leaves.
E1-05-darwin-finches-beak-adaptation

Darwin's finches: six finch heads arranged in an arc around a small map outline of the Galápagos Islands, each finch with a different beak shape. Large ground finch with a big deep beak next to a large hard seed; small ground finch with a small short beak next to small seeds; cactus finch with a long pointed beak next to a cactus flower; warbler finch with a thin pointed beak next to a small insect; woodpecker finch holding a cactus spine in a straight beak next to a tree bark grub; vegetarian finch with a parrot-like curved beak next to a bud. A small mainland ancestor finch at the top with arrows spreading out to the six.
E1-07-darwin-giraffe-neck-natural

Darwin's explanation of the giraffe's neck in three panels. Panel 1: a group of ancestral giraffes with a range of neck lengths (short, medium, slightly longer) standing under a tall acacia tree. Panel 2: during drought, the longer-necked giraffes feeding on high leaves while short-necked ones are thin and one lies dead. Panel 3: after many generations, a herd of long-necked giraffes.
E1-08-peppered-moth-industrial-melanism

Two side-by-side tree trunks. Left trunk: pale grey-green, covered in light lichen; a pale speckled peppered moth on it is almost invisible, while a dark moth on the same trunk stands out clearly, and a small bird approaches the dark moth. Right trunk: black and sooty, with a factory chimney and smoke in the background; the dark moth is almost invisible while the pale speckled moth stands out, and a bird approaches the pale moth.
E1-09-antibiotic-resistance-evolution-steps

Four petri-dish style circles in a left-to-right sequence showing antibiotic resistance. Circle 1: many blue bacteria with a few red (resistant) ones scattered among them. Circle 2: antibiotic capsule icon added; blue bacteria shown faded or burst, red ones intact. Circle 3: only red bacteria remaining, starting to divide. Circle 4: the circle full of red resistant bacteria.
E1-10-allopatric-speciation-stages

Speciation diagram in four horizontal stages. Stage 1: one population of brown beetles (or small birds) on a single landmass. Stage 2: a river or sea channel forms, dividing the landmass and the population into two groups. Stage 3: on the left side (dry and sandy), the group has become pale yellow; on the right side (forest), the group has become dark green, each with slightly different shapes. Stage 4: the barrier is gone, the two groups meet, but a red cross between them shows they cannot interbreed.
E1-02-redi-spontaneous-generation-experiment

Redi's experiment shown as three glass jars side by side, each containing a piece of red meat. Jar 1 is open, with flies landing on the meat and white maggots crawling on it. Jar 2 is sealed with a tight lid, the meat brownish but no maggots, flies outside. Jar 3 is covered with fine gauze, with flies sitting on the gauze, tiny eggs on top of the gauze and no maggots on the meat.
E1-03-pasteur-swan-neck-flask

Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment in three panels. Panel 1: a round glass flask of yellowish broth with a long S-shaped (swan) neck open at the end, over a flame, steam rising (boiling). Panel 2: the same flask cooled, with dust specks and tiny microbes trapped in the lowest bend of the neck; the broth clear. Panel 3: the neck broken off short, dust falling straight in, and the broth cloudy with microbes.
